lines: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea for 6 months
She presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
She reports a mild, persistent cough, especially when lying down, but denies any chest pain, palpitations, or lower extremity edema.
- Chronic heart failure (New York Heart Association Class III)
- History of acute rheumatic fever (childhood, age 8)
Her past medical history is significant for rheumatic fever during childhood.
- Father: Hypertension, cerebrovascular accident at age 70
- No family history of congenital heart disease or rheumatic fever
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Administrative assistant.
On physical examination, you note a diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.
A transthoracic echocardiogram reveals a thickened mitral valve with a narrowed orifice and doming of the anterior mitral leaflet during diastole.
Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is estimated to be 45 mmHg, while left ventricular end-diastolic pressure is within normal limits.
The patient's electrocardiogram shows signs of left atrial enlargement.

encounters.cc: Worsening dyspnea on exertion progressing to shortness of breath at rest with ankle swelling

lines: Worsening dyspnea on exertion progressing to shortness of breath at rest with ankle swelling
The patient returns for follow-up of rheumatic mitral stenosis, last evaluated in 2020, with progression of symptoms.
She reports reduced exercise tolerance, difficulty climbing stairs, and waking up at night gasping for air.
She also describes intermittent dry cough and recent swelling in her ankles.
She denies chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or orthopnea.
- Chronic heart failure (New York Heart Association Class III)
- History of acute rheumatic fever (childhood, age 8)
Her past medical history is significant for acute rheumatic fever in childhood, which required hospitalization but was not followed by long-term prophylaxis.
She has no known coronary artery disease or lung disease.
- Father: Hypertension, cerebrovascular accident at age 70
- No family history of congenital heart disease or rheumatic fever
She has no history of alcohol or drug use
Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 112/76 mm Hg, pulse is 84/min and regular, and respirations are 20/min.
On examination, she appears mildly dyspneic at rest.
Lung auscultation reveals bibasilar crackles without wheezes.
Cardiac examination reveals a loud S₂ and a grade 4/6 low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur best heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position, accentuated by handgrip.
The murmur is associated with a palpable thrill but no opening snap.
There is mild pitting edema of both ankles.
A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a thickened, immobile mitral valve with restricted opening and elevated left atrial pressures.
There is no significant mitral regurgitation or aortic valve abnormality.
ECG shows left atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.
